content: Our internet age has given rise to a fascinating phenomenon — social media influencers increasingly taking over the delivery of local news. They come in all shapes and sizes. There are the activists, political operators and even real estate agents. So many real estate agents. They also cover all sorts of things, from housing skirmishes to immigration enforcement to fistfights at In-N-Out locations. But what many of them have in common is a reach that often far outstrips that of traditional local media. Still, they aren’t replacing reporters altogether. They usually take cues or even full stories from local media outlets and repackage them in snippy social media videos that rack up thousands upon thousands of views. Sure, those videos are often rife with misinformation, or slanted to fit a political viewpoint, but that doesn’t necessarily impact the ballooning view counts. The whole thing poses a pretty existential question for journalism: Is it time to lean into influencer mode? Read the latest story in our Beef Week series here. Dem Party Opposes Recall of Dem Mayor The San Diego County Democratic Party’s Central Committee voted 50-11 to oppose the recall of Mayor Todd Gloria Tuesday night. Geneviéve Jones-Wright led a group of allies to file the recall and launch a website to gather interest and support . A coalition of unions and business leaders formed a committee to officially oppose the effort last week and draft the official response . (Times of San Diego) “In less than 12 months after a recall election would be scheduled, San Diegans will already have the opportunity to vote for a new mayor—with no additional recall expense or disruption to city government. That is the responsible, democratic, and fiscally sound path forward,” they wrote. No case actually for Gloria: When asked on CBS 8 about the recall effort, Gloria didn’t defend his record but instead also pointed to the cost: up to $12 million for a special recall election. “What I need your viewers to know is this is costly and risky for the city of San Diego,” he said. “This is seemingly intended to be very costly, create tremendous chaos — right out of Donald Trump’s playbook — at a time when we least need it.” The party also focused on the cost and didn’t say anything about Gloria’s leadership in its prepared statement. “A recall would be a toxic $16.5 million taxpayer-funded political knifefight that San Diego cannot afford. That money would be wasted on a divisive special election instead of roads, housing, public safety, and basic services,” read the statement. Jones-Wright told us that San Diego can’t wait for a change and criticized union leaders in particular. “You are telling impacted people, who have been harmed, that they need to just take it a little while longer. This people to show themselves: people who say they stand with working people are in this instance are turning their backs on those people,” she said. Culture Report: Venue Closures, Churches and Punk Shows There have been a whole lot of closures of artistic spaces in recent years. This month delivered two potential more: longtime hardcore venue Brick-by-Brick is changing hands and being renamed The Chevelle, while the historic one-screen independent theater La Paloma in Encinitas may be getting bought up by a church. That’s left our resident culturista Culture reporter Bella Ross “feeling like only two types of venues can be successful in San Diego right now: churches and anything involving lasers.” Her latest Culture Report digs into news of the closures and rounds up an eclectic list of arts and culture adjacent tidbits. Punk show at a bike co-op? Check. Questions about the future of Kobey’s swapmeet? Also check. Opportunity to get involved in a conversation about the future of San Diego’s troubled Pride nonprofit? Also check. Read the entire story here . Thankful for You! Thank you for reading the Morning Report. As we mentioned yesterday, you’ll still get the newsletter Friday, but it’s going to be a lighter version so we can spend time with our families. If you’re feeling generous, you can support our work here . Have a great Thanksgiving! In Other News Over the past two years, a small nonprofit has collected nearly 2,000 tons of trash from the Tijuana River. Now, as Southern California braces for a wetter winter and damaging high surf thanks to El Niño, the group’s “first line of defense” may be put to the test. (KPBS) San Diego city leaders are reviving efforts to bring a docked bike sharing network after previous programs died seven years ago due to controversy and complaints. (The Union-Tribune). From Oceanside to Imperial Beach, coastal communities may experience the tallest high tides on record over Thanksgiving weekend, with tides projected to reach higher than 8 feet. (The Union-Tribune). Opponents of a proposed, 150-mile San Diego Gas and Electric powerline are alleging in a new lawsuit that the operator broke state laws in order to become the project’s developer after it originally lost a competitive bid. (inewsource) As if our ME needed another reason to go to the mall, Westfield UTC has unveiled a new luxury wing. The owner’s latest investment hints at future plans for a “resort-inspired destination.” (Times of San Diego) Don’t feel like cooking today? No worries. San Diego Magazine has a list of restaurants offering Thanksgiving dinner on their menus. The Morning Report was written by Jakob McWhinney and Taylor O’Connor. title: The Blurring Line Between Local Influencers and Local News
summary: Our internet age has given rise to a fascinating phenomenon — social media influencers increasingly taking over the delivery of local news. The post The Blurring Line Between Local Influencers and Local News appeared first on Voice of San Diego .
content: Has your Realtor been acting kind of like a local news reporter, lately? David Wright is one of quite a few local real estate agents who dabble in the local media game. Just last week, he broke some pretty big news: San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria, after some renaming funny business, had finally passed the sales tax he wanted. “It’s official. Todd Gloria finally got his sales tax hike approved for you. The same act that didn’t pass in 2024, they basically just renamed it and made it nice and pretty as the Tijuana Clean Water Act. And Measure B now passed,” Wright explains while walking around a shopping center. Regular Voice of San Diego readers would be right to wonder why we haven’t covered Gloria’s new sales tax measure in our own pages. That would be because, well, it doesn’t exist. Measure B, it’s true, is a local sales tax voters passed earlier this month. But it didn’t have anything to do with Gloria. Measure B was a countywide sales tax, not a city one — remember, mayors lead cities — that will generate money for county government. The county Board of Supervisors will get that money and decide how to spend it; Gloria won’t see a dime. My point here is not to sound like an insufferable government nerd. It’s that Wright is one of what seems like a very fast growing number of amateurs doing local news on Instagram. Wright only has about 3,000 followers, but other accounts have found incredible success. Bern McGovern is a real estate agent doing mostly North County news with 80,000 followers. And it’s definitely not just real estate agents. An account called DaygoTV (323K followers) has more reach on Instagram than any traditional news outlet in San Diego. Beef Week is a Voice of San Diego reporting series. This week our newsroom will bringing you stories about all the beef and battles in San Diego. Read more Beef Week stories here. The relationship between amateur and professional reporters isn’t a fully formed beef. At its worst, it’s highly oppositional. Professional reporters sometimes feel the amateurs are stealing their content — and screwing up the most basic of facts along the way. The amateurs think reporters are stubbornly boring in their presentation — and not nearly invested enough in meeting audiences where they are, i.e. their feeds. At its best, though, it’s a relationship where both sides seem to be learning from the other. For real estate agents like McGovern, such big success has been a surprise. “It was definitely accidental,” said McGovern. He says that he was absolutely not setting out to be a reporter. Journalists at San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan’s press conference in the San Diego County District Attorney Press Room in downtown San Diego on Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2026. / Vito Di Stefano for Voice of San Diego Credit: Vito Di Stefano for Voice of San Diego “I was just talking about things going on as a local dad. That was my original angle. That’s still my angle,” he said. McGovern mostly covers local housing stories — and the fights that can ensue over whether new projects should be built. But nothing is really off limits. He covers restaurant openings and events around North County or really anything he guesses his audience might find interesting. Even though he started small and casual with a very small amount of followers, McGovern is perhaps the best local example of how a regular guy on Instagram (albeit articulate and charismatic) can get sucked into the vacuum created by a lack of local news. Generally speaking, McGovern follows around 10 different publications, he says. He’s constantly on alert for story lines that his viewers will find interesting and when he sees one, he throws a video together. It only takes him 20 to 30 minutes, he says. He talks over a green screen, drops his own image on top of some images of whatever he’s talking about and bam: journalism complete. In many cases, it took the reporter who wrote the original story quite a bit more than that — usually a story might take anywhere from several hours to several days. In that sense, he’s acting as what people in the news call an aggregator. You take the news someone else reported first and then you make a post about it and, hopefully, cite your sources. Aggregation isn’t necessarily bad; Voice of San Diego does it all the time. If you read our Morning Report, you’ll see that on a daily basis we are writing about news generated by other outlets. We always cite our sources and link back to their original reporting, which McGovern said he is doing in the vast majority of cases as well. McGovern said he frequently uses stories from Coast News about North County development to create his posts. I pointed out that, with his 80,000 followers, he now likely has a wider reach than the outlet whose news he is using. (Coast News has 21,000 followers on Instagram, but I have no idea of their print or online circulation.) McGovern said he has immense respect for what Coast News does. “I would be happy to help them in any way I can,” McGovern told me. “I’m surprised they don’t have their own people doing videos about their content.” He brings up a great point. Most of McGovern’s videos are extremely quick and dirty. He writes a short script, finds a few photos online, records a quick green screen video of himself and throws it all together. Successful amateurs like himself have exposed a massive hole in local news operations. It would not be terribly hard for reporters to take their 700-word written story, turn that into a 200-word script, record it and head home for the day. That asks reporters to do more with less, a mantra that’s already been killing them slowly for 20 years, and I don’t want to gloss over that. But most of us got into this business for the eyeballs. We want to influence the conversation. It’s a hell of a drug. Coast News — or any other local news outlet, including Voice — could have easily grabbed those 80,000 followers before McGovern if we’d been committed to meeting people where they are on the internet. While we could be studying McGovern’s tricks, successful amateurs like him have also been forced to study ours. Once accounts like McGovern’s start to blow up, people start reaching out to them asking them to look into things. Sometimes, now, they end up reporting their own original stories. That means making phone calls to people who know things, learning to use obscure government websites and tracking down documents — just like a “real” journalist. Emmett Egan, another local real estate agent, started posting just to make jokes online. More and more recently, he’s transitioned to doing local news and he says it has grown his account immensely. He now has about 31,000 followers on Instagram. When Egan is looking into a story, he’ll call anyone he thinks can help shed light on what he’s trying to find out. Even though he’s just a guy on social media, people usually speak to him, he says. “I feel like I got that from understanding what good news is. We’re learning from you guys,” he said. Egan, like McGovern, covers a lot of housing and tends to stay relatively neutral in his presentation, but the local news accounts proliferating on Instagram run the gamut in terms of what they cover and how. DaygoTV, San Diego’s biggest news account on Instagram, takes less of a curatorial approach and more of a kitchen sink approach. One of their recent posts is simply a repost of someone else: “First emails, now flights, tomorrow the internet gone.” Lol. A video a few days earlier shows a man, quite possibly on drugs or having a mental health episode, hanging out on top of a woman’s car like he is playing king of the hill. A much older post on DaygoTV’s backup account shows two grown men fighting at an In-N-Out in Chula Vista. “Thoughts on this?” the post asks. A note pinned to each post says everything anyone needs to know about DaygoTV’s news philosophy: “NSFW: This page does not intend to promote dangerous acts, organizations, violence, harassments, or bullying.” Figures. The internet has always been a place where the weird and outrageous rise to the surface. And before the internet, people made the same criticism about television. (For what it’s worth, NBC 7 appears to have the second largest Instagram following of any local news purveyor at about 247,000.) Amidst DaygoTV’s memes are a big sprinkling of what appear to be paid partnership posts promoting taco shops, car dealerships and mansion parties. DaygoTV does not differentiate between the paid advertisements and its regular posts — something that has historically been an important ethical distinction to professional news operations. A person operating the DaygoTV account declined to be interviewed for this story. Others accounts specialize in original reporting — meaning they’re constantly going out and gathering their own information, the same way mainstream reporters do. These accounts frequently have a strong political bent. Take Amy Reichert (113K followers) a conservative who previously ran for the county Board of Supervisors. Many liberals find her odious (she probably doesn’t mind) but it can’t be denied that Reichert does a fair amount of original information gathering. She pulled together a paper trail on childcare operations she thought might be committing fraud in San Diego. Another infamous influencer Nick Shirley came to town and teamed up with her and they eventually released a video. Several months later charges dropped. None of the childcare operations they put on film were charged with a crime, but one of the operations initially flagged by Reichert was. Then there’s Arturo Gonzalez (271K followers) who goes by @officialaturo on Instagram. Gonzalez gained a huge following during the massive wave of protests against police violence in 2020. (Maybe not surprisingly there is beef between he and Reichert.) Gonzalez lost his bag during the protests and then people followed along online as he tried to find it. The whole fiasco sparked a flurry of amazing memes about Gonzalez and his bag. Eventually, 30,000 people watched along as he was detained for unlawful assembly, as CBS 8 reported . Now Gonzalez specializes in tracking the movements of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He goes out and takes video himself and others also send him video, so he can alert communities when unmarked immigration vehicles are in their neighborhood. People are able to monetize their influence on Instagram to varying degrees. For real estate agents like McGovern and Egan, the payoff comes from the real estate clients they are able to reel in through presenting the news. McGovern said about 70 percent of his clients come from social media. One of the many subplots of the internet age has been the question of how professional news operations will make enough money to support their newsgathering into the future. Who knew the answer was as simple as getting a Realtor’s license. The post The Blurring Line Between Local Influencers and Local News appeared first on Voice of San Diego .
